pinterest.title: Trout Coconut Curry with Mustard Seeds and Curry Leaf
pinterest.description: This trout coconut curry poaches fresh mountain trout in a mustard seed, curry leaf, and coconut milk reduction. No heavy sauce, no falling-apart fish. The technique borrows from French poaching — gentle heat, controlled liquid — and the flavors are unambiguously South Asian. Firm, clean, on the table in 35 minutes. Full recipe at mubashirr.com.

instagram.caption:
Mountain trout deserves better than being fried into submission. This trout coconut curry starts with mustard seeds crackled in oil until they smell almost nutty, then curry leaves go in and the kitchen shifts — you know exactly where this is going. Coconut milk comes in low and slow. The trout is never boiled, never crowded. It poaches, barely simmering, and pulls out firm and clean, carrying the sauce without dissolving into it.

The technique is French in structure, South Asian in soul. I have made versions of this for years, adjusting the mustard-to-coconut ratio depending on whether I want something brighter or rounder. The version on the blog right now is where I have landed.

Thirty-five minutes. No resting time. No special equipment. Just a wide pan and fish you did not overcook.

Recipe is linked in bio. Make it on a weeknight when you want something that feels considered but does not ask much of you.

email.subject: Trout, mustard seeds, coconut milk
email.preheader: A 35-minute fish curry that does not fall apart on you.
email.body_html:
There is a version of fish curry that exists mostly as a warning — overcooked, waterlogged, the fish more suggestion than substance. This is not that.

The new recipe on the site is a trout coconut curry built on a specific sequence: mustard seeds crackled in oil, curry leaves added just after, then coconut milk brought in carefully and reduced before the fish ever touches the pan. By the time the trout goes in, the sauce already has structure. The poaching is gentle, controlled — a technique borrowed from French kitchens that happens to work perfectly with the South Asian spice base.

The result is fish that stays firm. Flakes when you press it, not when you look at it. A sauce that coats rather than floods.

A few things worth noting before you cook it:

  • Fresh curry leaves matter here. Dried ones will not do the same work.
  • The mustard seeds should pop and smell nutty, not burnt. Thirty seconds at most.
  • Coconut milk goes in on medium heat and stays there. This is not a dish for rushing the reduction.

Mountain trout is what I use. It holds up. A firm white fish would also work if trout is not available to you.

Thirty-five minutes, start to finish.

Read the full recipe and method here.

linkedin.body:
Most fusion cooking is additive — take a dish, throw something foreign at it, call it creative. The trout coconut curry I wrote about this week is not trying to do that.

The dish has a Pakistani spice logic at its core: mustard seeds, curry leaves, coconut milk, the sequencing of aromatics in hot oil. What it borrows from French technique is a single structural idea — that fish poached gently in a reduced, flavored liquid stays coherent. It does not disintegrate. It takes on flavor without surrendering texture.

That combination is not a gimmick. It is just good cooking. The French figured out gentle poaching for a reason. South Asian cooks figured out how to build fat-soluble flavor in the first thirty seconds of a dish for a reason. When those two ideas meet in the same pan, you do not get confusion — you get control.

I think about this when I write recipes: whether the technique is actually serving the ingredient, or whether it is there for the story. Here, the technique earns its place. The trout comes out firm. The sauce has body. The whole thing takes 35 minutes.

The recipe and the reasoning behind each step are on the blog if you want to read through it. The method is transferable to other firm white fish if trout is not something you have access to regularly.

tweets: Most fish curry recipes either overcook the fish or underbuild the sauce. I spent a while working out why, and the answer is mostly about when you add the fish and how hot the liquid is. This trout coconut curry is where that thinking landed.

The base is mustard seeds crackled in oil, then curry leaves, then coconut milk reduced slowly before the fish touches anything. By the time the trout goes in, the sauce already has structure. You are poaching into something, not boiling in nothing.

The technique is borrowed from French poaching — controlled heat, flavored liquid, short time. The spice logic is South Asian. Neither element is decorating the other. They are both doing actual work.

Trout holds up well here because it is firm and clean. The flesh does not fall apart. It flakes when it should, not before. If you have never poached fish in coconut milk, this is a good first time to try it.
35 minutes. Recipe and method are here: https://mubashirr.com/trout-coconut-curry-mustard-curry-leaf/
